verifications.claim: Over 1.3 million people have unclaimed 2022 federal tax refunds.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "over 1.3 million people across the nation have unclaimed refunds for tax year 2022" (R1, R2); "over 1.3 million individuals have approximately $1.2 billion in unclaimed refunds" (R3); "more than 1.3 million people nationwide still have not filed... leaving an estimated $1.2 billion in refunds unclaimed" (R6)
verifications.reasoning: Multiple sources directly state over 1.3 million people have unclaimed 2022 refunds, with exact figure 1,322,600 in tables.

verifications.claim: Unclaimed 2022 federal tax refunds total approximately $1.2 billion.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "approximately $1.2 billion in refunds remains unclaimed for taxpayers who have not filed their Form 1040... for the 2022 tax year" (R1, R2); "approximately $1.2 billion in unclaimed refunds" (R3); "estimated $1.2 billion in refunds unclaimed" (R6)
verifications.reasoning: Sources directly confirm approximately $1.2 billion (table total $1,159,244,200) for 2022 unclaimed refunds.

verifications.claim: The median unclaimed 2022 federal tax refund is $686.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "The IRS estimates the median refund amount is $686 for 2022" (R1, R2); "median refund of $686" (R3); "IRS estimates the median payout for unfiled 2022 returns is $686" (R6)
verifications.reasoning: Exact median figure $686 for 2022 unclaimed refunds stated directly in sources.

verifications.claim: Taxpayers have until April 15, 2025, to file their 2022 Form 1040 to claim unclaimed 2022 federal tax refunds.
verifications.label: INCORRECT
verifications.evidence: IR-2026-37, March 20, 2026: "face an April 15 deadline to submit their tax returns" for 2022 (R1, R2); "April 15 Deadline to Claim 2022 Tax Refunds (IR 2026-37)" (R3); "file overdue 2022 returns by the April 15 deadline" in 2026 context (R6)
verifications.reasoning: Sources specify April 15, 2026 deadline (IR-2026-37 context) for 2022 refunds, directly contradicting 2025.

verifications.claim: Unclaimed 2022 federal tax refunds become the property of the U.S. Treasury after April 15, 2025.
verifications.label: INCORRECT
verifications.evidence: "If they do not file within three years, the money becomes the property of the U.S. Treasury" tied to April 15, 2026 deadline (R1, R2); "after which unclaimed amounts become property of the U.S. Treasury" post-April 15, 2026 (R3); "window shuts this April" (2026) (R6)
verifications.reasoning: Treasury forfeiture after three years/April 15, 2026 for 2022, contradicting specified 2025 date.

verifications.claim: The law requires a 3-year window to file and claim refunds.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "Under the law, taxpayers usually have three years to file and claim their tax refunds" (R1, R2, R6); "Under the law, individuals generally have three years to file returns and claim refunds" (R3); "a return claiming a refund must be filed within three years" (R4); "IRS is required to keep the filing open... for three years" (R5); "within three years of the filing deadline" (R7)
verifications.reasoning: All relevant sources confirm general 3-year legal window for claiming refunds.

verifications.claim: Federal tax refunds can be used to pay off outstanding federal or state debts such as child support or student loans.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "any refund for 2022 will be applied to amounts still owed to the IRS or a state tax agency and may be used to offset unpaid child support or other past due federal debts, such as student loan debts" (R1, R2, R6); "refunds may be reduced or offset against outstanding federal or state liabilities, including unpaid taxes, child support, or student loans" (R3); similar for 2021 (R4)
verifications.reasoning: Sources directly state refunds offset debts including child support and student loans.

verifications.claim: There is generally no penalty for failing to file if a refund is due.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "There is no penalty for failure to file if a refund is due." (R4)
verifications.reasoning: Direct statement in R4 confirms general rule; consistent with IRS policy though not repeated in 2022-specific sources.
